title: The Disappearance of Dorothy Arnold
summary: Unsolved mystery edition of Stuff You Should Know on the 1910 disappearance of New York socialite Dorothy Arnold, who vanished on December 12, 1910 after going dress shopping in Manhattan. The hosts cover her family background and literary ambitions, the investigation led by attorney John Keith, Pinkerton detectives and the NYPD, the press coverage and false leads (ocean liner brochures, fake ransom letters, postcards), her secret romance with George S. Griscom Jr. and the Cambridge/Boston trip, the son John's confrontation with Griscom in Italy, and later theories and sightings including a 1914 Pittsburgh abortion-clinic raid, a Rhode Island prisoner's claim, a 1921 police captain's remark, and the Anna Miller look-alike in Kansas City. The episode closes with the destruction of Dorothy's letters by her niece Rebecca and a listener mail segment correcting a Patrick Dempsey movie reference.
topics: Stuff You Should Know unsolved mystery

segments.title: Unsolved mystery edition intro
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the unsolved mystery edition and call the Dorothy Arnold case one of the oldest missing persons cases still open in New York City.

segments.title: Dorothy Arnold's background
segments.summary: Dorothy Harriet Camille Arnold, daughter of perfume importer Francis Arnold, grew up wealthy on East 79th Street, had Mayflower lineage and a Supreme Court justice uncle, and wanted to be a writer in Greenwich Village. Her family discouraged her ambitions.

segments.title: Family opposition to her writing
segments.summary: Her father refused to let her move to Greenwich Village. Her McClure's magazine story submissions were rejected and mocked, so she used a secret P.O. box.

segments.title: Day of disappearance: dress shopping
segments.summary: On December 12, 1910, Dorothy left to buy a dress for her sister's debutante ball with about thirty dollars. She walked down Fifth Avenue, stopped at other shops, bought chocolates and a book charged to her father's account, and no dress shop visit is known.

segments.title: Last sighting and family worry
segments.summary: Dorothy met a friend in the afternoon and said she would walk through Central Park, the last known sighting. When she missed dinner, the family quietly made calls to her friends amid fear of scandal.

segments.title: Family secrecy and a false report
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a similar earlier case of a runaway socialite and the family's motives for secrecy. A friend was told by her mother that Dorothy had come home with a headache, which was untrue.

segments.title: Hiring investigators and going to police
segments.summary: The family hired attorney John Keith, who searched records and suggested a Pinkerton detective. After ten days they went to Deputy Police Commissioner William J. Flynn, who issued a silent alarm to keep the case out of the press.

segments.title: Public announcement and reward
segments.summary: On January 25, police held a press conference and offered a thousand dollar reward. The New York Times ran the story under a headline referencing the niece of Justice Peckham.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Runaway theories and ocean liner leads
segments.summary: Police initially thought she ran off to marry, based on ocean liner brochures, which led nowhere after the company checked passenger records. Speculation ranged from elopement to suicide to murder, and false sightings and fake ransom letters arrived.

segments.title: Fake postcard and family's views
segments.summary: Reporters said she would return soon, and the family's and press's reports were contradicted. The father believed she was dead, and a postcard claiming she was safe was thought to be a hoax.

segments.title: Mother's health and Griscom revealed
segments.summary: The family said Mary was in a New Jersey rest home. Dorothy turned up in Italy searching for George S. Griscom Jr., 15 years older, unemployed Harvard graduate. The father had said he would prefer she see men of position and business.

segments.title: Boston rendezvous and hotel registration
segments.summary: Dorothy went to Cambridge and Boston to meet Griscom under a pretext of visiting a college friend, pawning jewelry for about $500 in 1910 money. The hosts disagree on why she registered at the Lenox under her own name while Griscom stayed at the Essex.

segments.title: Griscom in Italy and the letters
segments.summary: Griscom was on vacation with elderly parents in Italy. Mary and son John confronted him, and John beat him up and took letters Dorothy had mailed. Griscom later returned and aided the search, and Dorothy's letter saying failure stared her in the face and 'mother will always think an accident has happened' came to light.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Griscom's conflicting statements and worldwide search
segments.summary: Griscom returned on February 9 with changing accounts of their relationship and claimed she would return. Police asked for the letters, which were said to be destroyed. A worldwide search followed, and newspapers continued covering the case for years.

segments.title: 1914 Pittsburgh abortion raid and 1921 police claim
segments.summary: In 1914 a Pittsburgh-area hospital raid led a doctor to imply Dorothy died during an illegal abortion and was cremated; nothing came of it. In 1921 NYPD Bureau of Missing Persons Captain J.H. Ayers said police knew what happened, then retracted it.

segments.title: Rhode Island prisoner claim and Central Park search
segments.summary: A Rhode Island State Prison inmate claimed he had been paid to dispose of Dorothy's body in a West Point, New York cellar; police dug and found nothing. The Central Park reservoir was also dragged with no evidence found.

segments.title: Amnesia theory
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the theory that Dorothy suffered amnesia from a head injury, which they say is speculative.

segments.title: Anna Miller of Kansas City
segments.summary: In the 1930s, New York police traveled to Kansas City after sightings and found Anna Miller, wife of a movie projector operator, who looked nearly identical to Dorothy, had the same birthmark, said she had moved from New York on December 12, 1910, and had a Fifth Avenue fur and muffler. Police were satisfied she was not Dorothy.

segments.title: Theories of suicide and a bohemian escape
segments.summary: John Keith believed she took her own life, while historian Sylvia Petim first favored a botched abortion and later thought she disappeared to escape her family. The hosts discuss whether good spirits rule out suicide.

segments.title: Father's search cost and the destroyed letters
segments.summary: Francis Arnold spent about a dozen years and a million 1920s dollars searching. Mary died six years later. Niece Rebecca, heir to the papers, destroyed Dorothy's letters, so family descendants do not know what happened.

segments.title: Wrap-up and transition
segments.summary: The hosts say the case will likely never be solved and move on to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Patrick Dempsey movie correction
segments.summary: Listener Alex Thompson corrected a quote attributed to Can't Buy Me Love that the hosts said was from Loverboy. The hosts discuss the two films and whether Can't Buy Me Love has nudity.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Credits and sign-off.
